name: Bigthan and Teresh
charge: Two of the king’s chamberlains, of those which kept the door, being wroth and seeking to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus
summary: While Mordecai sat in the king’s gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king’s chamberlains who kept the door, were angry and sought to kill king Ahasuerus (Esther 2:21). Mordecai learned of it and told Esther, who told the king in Mordecai’s name; the matter was searched out, both men were put to death, and it was written in the chronicles (Esther 2:22-23; Rest of Esther 12:1-3). That record came up years later on a sleepless night and turned Haman’s plot back on his own head (Esther 6:1-11).
offenseFull: Mordecai, a Benjamite carried away from Jerusalem with Jeconiah, raised Esther, his uncle’s daughter, as his own, and when she was made queen she still kept his charge not to show her people (Esther 2:5-7; Esther 2:10; Esther 2:20). The class teaches that they were cousins, not uncle and niece, and that they came of the mighty Benjamite line of Kish, the same line as Saul (1 Samuel 9:1-2). Mordecai served in the king’s court and sat in the king’s gate.

In those days two of the king’s chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, of those who kept the door, were angry and sought to lay hands on king Ahasuerus (Esther 2:21): a coup against the king by men trusted to guard him. The Rest of Esther calls them Gabatha and Tharra, two eunuchs of the king and keepers of the palace, and the teaching explains that chamberlains were eunuchs, made so that they would not lie with the women they kept (Rest of Esther 12:1). Mordecai heard their devices and searched out their purposes before he spoke (Rest of Esther 12:2). The same chapter says that Haman the Agagite, already in great honour with the king, sought to harm Mordecai and his people because of the two eunuchs (Rest of Esther 12:6). The teaching draws the line from there: Greece was always trying to overthrow Persia, Haman’s aim was to translate the kingdom of the Persians to the Macedonians, and the two eunuchs were part of that plan (Rest of Esther 16:12-14). Asked in class whether Haman was plotting with them, the teacher answered that he possibly was.
judgmentFull: The thing was known to Mordecai, who told Esther the queen, and Esther told the king in Mordecai’s name; when the matter was searched out it was found true, both men were hanged on a tree, and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king (Esther 2:22-23). The Rest of Esther adds that the king examined them, that after they confessed they were strangled, and that he rewarded Mordecai with service in the court (Rest of Esther 12:3-5). The teaching holds the two records together: they were strangled, they were hung on a tree. Mordecai told, and the class says that is what a man is supposed to do. Israel in captivity was commanded to seek the peace of the city where they were carried and to pray for it, for in its peace they would have peace, which is why Mordecai kept the king safe (Jeremiah 29:7).

These nations kept records, and so did Israel, and the study note marks that this deed of Mordecai’s would later help the whole nation. On the night Haman came to ask for Mordecai’s death, the king could not sleep, had the chronicles read, found that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, and learned that nothing had been done for him (Esther 6:1-3). The teaching calls the Lord a mastermind in how He moves, using even a king’s sleeplessness to set His purpose in motion. Haman, asked what should be done for the man the king wished to honour, described the highest honour he could think of, sure it was for himself, and was made to parade Mordecai through the city in it (Esther 6:4-11). What Haman planned for himself was given to the man he hated.

text.text: In those days, while Mordecai sat in the king’s gate, two of the king’s chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, of those which kept the door, were wroth, and sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus.
And the thing was known to Mordecai, who told it unto Esther the queen; and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai’s name.
And when inquisition was made of the matter, it was found out; therefore they were both hanged on a tree: and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king.
And Mardocheus took his rest in the court with Gabatha and Tharra, the two eunuchs of the king, and keepers of the palace.
And he heard their devices, and searched out their purposes, and learned that they were about to lay hands upon Artexerxes the king; and so he certified the king of them.
Then the king examined the two eunuchs, and after that they had confessed it, they were strangled.
On that night could not the king sleep, and he commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles; and they were read before the king.
And it was found written, that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king’s chamberlains, the keepers of the door, who sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus.
And the king said, What honour and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this? Then said the king’s servants that ministered unto him, There is nothing done for him.
And the king said, Who is in the court? Now Haman was come into the outward court of the king’s house, to speak unto the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him.
And the king’s servants said unto him, Behold, Haman standeth in the court. And the king said, Let him come in.

So Haman came in. And the king said unto him, What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour? Now Haman thought in his heart, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?
And Haman answered the king, For the man whom the king delighteth to honour,
Let the royal apparel be brought which the king useth to wear, and the horse that the king rideth upon, and the crown royal which is set upon his head:

And let this apparel and horse be delivered to the hand of one of the king’s most noble princes, that they may array the man withal whom the king delighteth to honour, and bring him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaim before him, Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour.

Then the king said to Haman, Make haste, and take the apparel and the horse, as thou hast said, and do even so to Mordecai the Jew, that sitteth at the king’s gate: let nothing fail of all that thou hast spoken.

Then took Haman the apparel and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaimed before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour.
Now in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite;
Who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity which had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away.

And he brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle’s daughter: for she had neither father nor mother, and the maid was fair and beautiful; whom Mordecai, when her father and mother were dead, took for his own daughter.
Esther had not shewed her people nor her kindred: for Mordecai had charged her that she should not shew it.
Esther had not yet shewed her kindred nor her people; as Mordecai had charged her: for Esther did the commandment of Mordecai, like as when she was brought up with him.
Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Bechorath, the son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, a mighty man of power.

And he had a son, whose name was Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people.
And Mardocheus took his rest in the court with Gabatha and Tharra, the two eunuchs of the king, and keepers of the palace.
And he heard their devices, and searched out their purposes, and learned that they were about to lay hands upon Artexerxes the king; and so he certified the king of them.
Howbeit Aman the son of Amadathus the Agagite, who was in great honour with the king, sought to molest Mardocheus and his people because of the two eunuchs of the king.
But he, not bearing his great dignity, went about to deprive us of our kingdom and life:

Having by manifold and cunning deceits sought of us the destruction, as well of Mardocheus, who saved our life, and continually procured our good, as also of blameless Esther, partaker of our kingdom, with their whole nation.
For by these means he thought, finding us destitute of friends to have translated the kingdom of the Persians to the Macedonians.

And the king made a record of these things, and Mardocheus also wrote thereof.
So the king commanded, Mardocheus to serve in the court, and for this he rewarded him.
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the Lord for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
